targetQuery: virtual memory paging TLB explained (with .NET/C# working set measurement)
comparedAgainst: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/memory/virtual-address-space, about-memory-management, reserving-and-committing-memory, working-set (Microsoft Learn conceptual docs, also this article's own cited sources) — fetched and quote-checked directly. Purely conceptual, C/C++-only sample code (SEH-based VirtualAlloc loop), no .NET angle, no working-set/private/virtual triad tied together in one program, no memory-mapped files. Every quote the article attributes to these pages was verified verbatim (8 TB figure, working-set definition, hard/soft/demand-zero fault taxonomy, 'committed pages do not consume any physical storage until they are first accessed'); no close paraphrase found beyond the article's own attributed quotes.

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/io/memory-mapped-files and .../memorymappedfile.createnew — fetched directly. Has C# code, but Microsoft's own non-persisted-file example is a three-process, Mutex-synchronized Process-A/B/C console app. This article's two-view-accessor demo (single process, GUID temp file) and its CreateNew-name-collision/CreateOrOpen-fix demo are original constructions with different structure, variable names and narrative — not reused from Microsoft's sample.

https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/operating-systems/virtual-memory-in-operating-system/ — top-ranking generic OS-course overview for the topic. No code of any kind, no measured numbers, no TLB/working-set/page-table technical depth (confirmed by fetch: page fault formula and a page/puzzle-piece analogy is the extent of its rigor). Thin by comparison on every axis.

OSTEP (Arpaci-Dusseau) chapters 18 and 19, https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/vm-paging.pdf and vm-tlbs.pdf — read in full (not just the citation snippet). The book's own array-indexing example (VPN=1, PFN=7, virtual address 21) and its own TLB hit/miss homework microbenchmark (Figure 19.5, 'roughly a factor of fourteen') are both real and match the article's citations exactly. The article's own worked exercise (page number 0x4A/frame 0x37, address 0x0004A1F3) and its own TLB-cost framing are original, not reused from the book's example.
justification:
On research quality this is exceptional: every one of the twelve cited pages was independently fetched and checked, and every quoted or paraphrased claim attributed to Microsoft Learn or OSTEP matches the source exactly, including the least-obvious ones (the 8 TB figure is on 'About Memory Management', not 'Virtual Address Space', and the article cites it correctly; the OSTEP 'roughly fourteen times' TLB miss/hit ratio is a real, specific number from the book's own Figure 19.5 homework measurement, correctly hedged as 'the general shape to expect... specific to that measurement and that hardware'). run-code.mjs confirms PASS blocks=10 executed=5, matching the writer's claim exactly. The VirtualAlloc/VirtualFree P/Invoke demo and both MemoryMappedFile demos are original code: they differ structurally from Microsoft's own SEH-based C++ sample and from Microsoft's Mutex-synchronized three-process sample respectively, and no other tutorial-style source turned up matching phrasing or code shape. Structure is genuinely different from the sibling processes-and-threads.md (that article's seven headings are all statement-form; this one's are six literal interrogatives plus one contrastive title), and the opening paragraph explicitly extends rather than repeats that article's child-process experiment. The three exercises are three different forms (a hex-arithmetic prove-it, an extend-the-code-and-predict, and a colleague's-bug find-the-bug), matching the writer's claim. The Task Manager hedge is handled well: the article asserts exact Performance Monitor counter names only where it can verify them (all three confirmed against the live .NET API docs — 'Working Set', 'Private Bytes', 'Virtual Bytes' are the literal counter names given on those pages), and deliberately stops short of asserting Task Manager's column label strings, which reads as careful, not evasive. No filler, no ad code, no keyword stuffing, and the toolchain statement ('Measured on .NET 10.0.401, Windows 11, x64') sits immediately before the first real measurement rather than in the opening paragraph, as required.

Against that, the article's own closing section contains a clear, checkable numerical error that an AdSense-style reviewer would catch on a re-read, and it undercuts the 'every number is real' trust the rest of the piece earns. The closing section says the baseline virtual figure (2,233,454 MB, given earlier in the article) was 'tens of thousands of times the installed RAM' (63.9 GB) and that '[e]very 64-bit process starts with most of an 8 TB address space nominally available.' Recomputing from the article's own numbers: 2,233,454 MB / (63.9 GB x 1024) is about 34, not tens of thousands (three orders of magnitude off); and 2,233,454 MB is about 26.6% of an 8 TB (8,388,608 MB) address space, not 'most' of it. Both are overstatements built from numbers the article itself supplied a few paragraphs earlier, which is exactly the kind of avoidable, checkable error that makes a reader distrust the rest of the piece's numbers even though everything else checked out. This is a single, isolated defect in an otherwise very strong article, but it sits in the article's rhetorical payoff paragraph, so it is not a minor nit. Held below the 8.5 pass line for this reason; everything else here would otherwise support a 9.0-9.5.

issues.location: Closing section, "Does a multi-terabyte 'virtual' figure mean the machine is almost out of memory?", the sentence beginning "the virtual number was already tens of thousands of times the installed RAM" and the following sentence "Every 64-bit process starts with most of an 8 TB address space nominally available"
issues.problem: Both quantitative comparisons are wrong by the article's own numbers. Baseline VirtualMemorySize64 was measured earlier as roughly 2,233,454 MB, and RAM was measured as 63.9 GB (= 65,433.6 MB). 2,233,454 / 65,433.6 is approximately 34, not 'tens of thousands' (off by roughly three orders of magnitude). Separately, 2,233,454 MB is about 26.6% of an 8 TB (8,388,608 MB) address space, which is a quarter, not 'most' of it. These are checkable arithmetic errors built from numbers the article itself supplied, not fabricated facts, but they read exactly like an overstated, unsupported claim to a policy reviewer, and they undercut trust in the article's other (correctly wildcarded and scoped) measured numbers.
issues.fixLooksLike: Recompute both comparisons from the article's own baseline numbers and either state the correct order of magnitude (roughly 30-40x the installed RAM; roughly a quarter of the 8 TB address space) or drop the specific multiplier/fraction and keep only the qualitative point that virtual space is nominally available almost for free regardless of installed RAM, without a false numeric anchor.
